5.title: What Minority Report got right about AI
5.author: Patrick Neeman
5.description:
Steven Spielberg’s Precogs Are The Sharpest Portrait Of Generative AI Anyone Drew Before It Arrived — Fluent, Confident, Acting On Their Own, Hallucinations Included.

Watch Minority Report again and count what people quote from it and the answer is always the same: Tom Cruise in a black glove, waving his hands at a floating screen, conducting video like an orchestra. That image launched a thousand concept demos and a generation of gesture-controlled ambition.

It is also the least accurate thing the film predicted.

The 2002 movie, directed by Steven Spielberg and lifted from Philip K. Dick’s 1956 story The Minority Report, is remembered as a design showpiece. Look past the interface everyone copied and you find something more exact: a sketch of generative artificial intelligence.

The precogs do not look the future up in a database, they generate it by producing a fluent, confident account of what will happen, which the system treats as fact.

Swap the psychics for a language model and the machinery is identical, down to the failure the plot is built on.

That is not set dressing, it is the product specification for the tool in hundreds of millions of pockets, warning label included. The precogs were never the villains.

Read as design fiction rather than spectacle, they are the most accurate portrait of generative AI anyone drew before it arrived.

The Gesture Interface Was the Decoy

Of all the futures the film put on screen, the gesture interface is the one designers took home.

Christopher Noessel and Nathan Shedroff, who cataloged science-fiction interfaces in Make It So, describe the precog scrubber in What Sci-Fi Tells Interaction Designers About Gestural Interfaces as one of the most referenced interfaces in cinematic history. Every product person who has mimed pinch-and-swipe in a pitch owes it a royalty.

Then it aged into a gimmick.

https://medium.com/media/612c2079426ff989b7e667c5dba16011/href

Waving your arms at a vertical screen is exhausting inside a minute, and the industry had named the problem “gorilla arm” before Cruise put on the glove.

In 2010, Don Norman and Jakob Nielsen warned in Gestural Interfaces: A Step Backwards in Usability that the rush toward “natural” gestures was throwing out decades of hard-won standards — visibility, feedback, a reliable way to undo. The interfaces that won instead shrank to a slab of glass, then a voice, then a text box that answers back.

The most copied idea in the film was the one that mattered least.

Designers copy what photographs well, and a gloved hand sweeping through light is a poster while a model quietly generating a confident answer is not. So the poster got mimicked in keynote after keynote while the generative engine got built off camera.

A science-fiction interface is made to be read in two seconds, not operated for two hours — Cruise sweeps his arms because the camera needs to see him think. Believable and usable are different problems, and cinema only has to solve the first.

The same misdirection is happening again, except today the copied thing is the chat box. Change the input device all you like — glove, mouse, voice, prompt — and the hard question underneath does not move. It is what you do with an answer a machine invented and delivered without a flicker of doubt.

The Precogs Were a Generative Model

Strip the film to its plumbing and the precogs are a generative model with a homicide division. They do not retrieve a fact about the future; they synthesize one that did not exist until they generated it. Ask a language model a question and it does not look up the answer either — it generates the most plausible continuation, token by token, and hands it over with the calm authority the precogs give their visions.

For most of the film’s life that looked like fantasy. ChatGPT crossed 800 million weekly users within three years of launch, and generative models are now wired into search, email, coding tools, and the support box on half the sites you visit.

A decade ago the answer to a question was a list of links you weighed yourself; now it is one generated paragraph that has done the weighing and shows you none of it.

The precogs do not retrieve the future; they generate it, the same move that makes a language model useful and needs human in the loop.

The distinction matters more than it sounds.

  • A search engine retrieves, and when it has nothing it returns nothing — the blank is honest.
  • A generative model never returns a blank; it still produces a plausible, well-formed answer, because that is the only thing it does.

Confidence is not a signal that the system is right, it is the house style. The model gets treated as a component that returns answers, the way a database returns rows, and the difference between looking something up and making it up never comes up.

That difference is the product risk.

Josh Clark has a name for the version of this we now live inside. In Say Hello to Sentient Design, he and Veronika Kindred argue that generative interfaces are already here rather than on the way, and that we meet machine-made output dozens of times a day without registering it.

A machine producing confident answers about matters it cannot verify is now the ordinary condition.

The Precogs Were the Training Data

Now the part people find hardest to sit with. The precogs are not machines — they are three people, drugged, floating in a tank, their minds strip-mined for visions they never volunteered. Precrime’s marketing calls them a system, the state keeps them in a room the public never sees, and the apparatus rests on human beings whose contribution is compulsory and uncredited.

That is the origin question generative AI keeps trying not to answer, and the interface is exactly where the answer gets hidden.

A model’s fluency is not conjured; it is distilled from an enormous quantity of human work gathered without asking, and the bill is arriving in court. A federal judge gave final approval in 2026 to Anthropic’s $1.5 billion settlement with authors over pirated books, roughly $3,000 per work across some 500,000 works — the largest copyright recovery on record. The New York Times’ case against OpenAI heads toward trial on the same question.

The tank is not a metaphor, and every fluent answer is somebody’s labor, rendered anonymous under fair use.

It is not only the writing that got absorbed, either. TIME reported that OpenAI’s contractors in Kenya were paid between $1.32 and $2 an hour to read the worst material on the internet so ChatGPT would not repeat it.

People took the toxicity directly so the output could feel clean. The film has a precise image for that arrangement, and it is not flattering.

For designers the point is not guilt, it is disclosure. Interfaces are built to make generated output feel like it came from nowhere, and that seamlessness is a choice. Linking what the model drew on, marking which parts are retrieved and which invented — these are design decisions, and defaulting to silence about where an answer came from is the instinct that kept the tank out of sight.

The System Acts and Nobody Checks

The precogs’ visions do not sit in a report. They trigger an arrest — a team acts on the generated output before the predicted event has happened, generation and action welded together.

That weld is what the industry is racing to build, and it has a name: agents. PwC found that 79 percent of companies already have AI agents in use, tools that generate a plan and then execute it without waiting to be asked.

The dazzle is real, and so is the quiet transfer of authority, because each capability added is a decision handed to a system that generates its confidence as fluently as its answers. Every agent demo I have watched ends at the moment of success, never at someone unpicking what it did on a bad day.

The prompt box kept a person between the generated answer and the world. The agent’s whole selling point is removing them.

The prompt box kept a person between the generated answer and the world. The agent’s whole selling point is removing them.

Watch what the precrime cops do with all that automation. They do not investigate; they receive a name, confirm it on a screen, and make the arrest, with the detective work handed off to the oracle entirely. That is automation bias, the tendency to over-trust a machine and stop checking it.

A 2023 study in Scientific Reports found people defer to an AI recommendation even when it is visibly wrong, then keep making its mistakes after the system is switched off. Generative AI sharpens this, because fluency reads as competence.

Ben Shneiderman argues this is a false choice. In Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence: Reliable, Safe & Trustworthy, he replaces the usual dial — more automation, less human control — with two axes and puts the goal where both run high.

Precrime sits in the opposite corner, and the rule it breaks is worth stating plainly: match the reversibility of the action to your confidence in the generation. A draft left for you to send is cheap to be wrong about, a sent email is not, a payment is less so, and an arrest is catastrophic.

The fix is not less capability but deliberate friction: show the two answers the model was torn between, and make someone type a consequential decision rather than click accept.

The Minority Report Was the Hallucination

Here is the part with the film’s name on it. A “minority report” is what happens when the precogs disagree — one generates a different outcome, and the system buries the dissent to present a single clean verdict. That suppression is the plot, and it is also a design decision. Anderton gets flagged as a future murderer, and the vision that would clear him is filed away, because the system is built to output certainty rather than doubt.

That is hallucination, described twenty years early. A generative model also discards the cloud of things it could have said and hands you one answer with the uncertainty stripped off. When that answer is wrong but fluent, it is a minority report the system declined to show you.

And it is not rare. Stanford researchers tested the legal AI tools sold specifically as grounded and hallucination-free, reporting in Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools that Lexis+ AI and Westlaw’s tool still fabricate or misstate the law between 17 and 33 percent of the time, and those are the careful, retrieval-grounded systems.

Generated prose compounds it, flattening the difference between what the model knew and what it invented, so the retrieved citation and the fabricated one sit in the same sentence.

A model confident enough to answer is confident enough to be wrong about a person.

A model confident enough to answer is confident enough to be wrong about a person. So build the minority report back in on purpose. This is not new advice — Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction, published by Saleema Amershi and colleagues at Microsoft in 2019, tells you to make plain what a system can and cannot do and to support correction when it is wrong.

In practice: surface the uncertainty, show the sources beside the answer, and give the person a path to contest it before the system acts. It rarely happens because certainty ships faster than doubt, so teams round the confidence up and let the prose imply a sureness the model never earned.

Two questions cut through this on any generative feature.

  • What does it show when the model is unsure, and who absorbs the cost when it is fluently wrong?
  • If the answers are nothing and someone outside the room, you have shipped precrime with better typography.

The Real Forecast Was Never on the Screen

The film got the spectacle wrong and the substance right, which is the usual ratio for design fiction. We copied the gloves and missed the machine.

For two decades, “it’s like Minority Report” meant waving at a screen, when the truer read was the opposite — a system generating confident answers about a world it could not see, and people acting on them before anyone checked.

That future arrived, and it did not stay in the lab — It writes hundreds of millions of answers a week, drafts the email, runs the query, and increasingly acts without asking.

The edge case the film built its plot around is no longer hypothetical; it is a measured rate, aimed at people, not playlists.

The work now is not to build the generative engine; that part is done. The work is to build the minority report back into it — to treat the model’s suppressed uncertainty as a feature, not a bug, and to keep a human between the generated answer and the consequence. Watch the film again. Skip the hands. Study what the machine was so sure about, and who paid when it turned out wrong.

What Minority Report got right about AI was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

6.title: You can’t grow roses in a cornfield
6.author: Vlad Derdeicea
6.description:
A conversation with Whitney Hess, on careers, whispers, and where to plant yourself

Some questions sound administrative but are not, and “why do you want to switch jobs?” turns out to be one of them. I asked it on a mentoring call in the way you would ask about notice periods or portfolio order, one practical item among several, and the designer on my screen began to cry. Neither of us expected it. We sat with it for a moment, the way you do when a video call suddenly contains something real, and when she tried to answer, the answer had very little to do with jobs.

I brought this moment to Whitney Hess, who spent a decade as one of the most visible independent UX consultants of that era, based in New York for much of it with clients around the world, before consciously shifting her business from consulting to coaching, and who has therefore listened to more designers talk about their careers than almost anyone alive. She was not surprised. Long before people can say out loud that the work no longer fits, she told me, they hear it as a whisper: a quiet, dismissible sense that this is not what they want. The whisper is patient. Left unanswered it does not fade but grows, until one day it has become a daily shout, and a person finds herself crying on an ordinary mentoring call without quite knowing how she got there.

I have been interviewing designers who left the craft, or reshaped it into something new, for a book I am slowly writing about what is happening to our profession. Whitney is firmly in the second camp, and she will correct you if you suggest otherwise: she has never left UX, and she keeps her identity as a UX designer today. What she changed was the shape of the work, and she changed it while everything was still going up: the clients were blue-chip, the blog was widely read, the field itself was ascendant. That is what makes her worth listening to now. Most of us only examine what we really want when circumstances force the question, and she examined it voluntarily, at the height of a thriving practice, while the whisper was still at whisper volume. Since it is the quiet season, and half the industry is out of office with more time to think than usual, her story seems worth telling at length.

What the whisper actually says

Whitney’s move out of consulting was not a leap, and it did not begin with dissatisfaction. She registered her company in 2005, went fully independent about three years later, and built the kind of practice most designers would consider a destination: Scientific American, WNYC, the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum. The trouble, when it arrived, arrived inside the work rather than around it. “I wasn’t really addressing the systemic problems” she told me. A project would end, the deliverable would be good, and the organization that received it would remain exactly the organization it had been before. So she began pulling her clients’ own teams deeper into the work, partly for better outcomes and partly because, as she put it, it “felt weird not leaving the company in a better place.”

It is worth noticing what the whisper was actually saying, because it was not saying quit; it was saying something more precise. It was telling her which part of the work was hers: less the solving than the facilitating, less the deliverable than the people gathered around it. The signs were public long before she acted on them. In 2012 she wrote on her blog that her consulting role had become “kind of like that of a group-therapist,” which reads today like a diagnosis published in plain sight; within eight months of writing it she had enrolled in a yearlong coaching training. The certification did not change what she was. It caught up with what she had already become.

The biggest challenge is how you design your career.

The economics of listening

The economics deserve to be told plainly, because this is the part that career-change stories usually leave out, and because Whitney, it turns out, has crossed twice.

The first crossing was the raw one. In 2008, after three years of running her consulting business on the side, she left her full-time job to make it her whole livelihood, and the numbers underneath that decision were thin: about three months of savings, in New York, with no institutional net. “It was terrifying,” she told me, and she meant it concretely enough that she had decided she would work at Starbucks if that was what staying independent required. What she had instead of a cushion was a track record of a particular kind. “I’ve always trusted my ability to figure it out,” she said. “I knew I was going to be resourceful.” Designers will recognize that sentence, because it describes the psychological posture of every project we have ever started: a new domain, unclear requirements, stakeholders we have never met, and a working assumption that within a few weeks we will understand the problem better than the people who handed it to us. It is a strange kind of confidence, empirical rather than temperamental, assembled from having been dropped into the unknown many times and having found the shape of it each time. Whitney’s real innovation was pointing that confidence at her own livelihood.

The second crossing, into coaching in 2013 and 2014, looked nothing like the first, and the difference is the lesson. By then she had significantly more savings, and she kept taking UX consulting projects while the coaching practice ramped up, winding one income down as the other grew. The first crossing she survived on nerve; the second she designed. In time the coaching revenue found its footing, and the consulting decade turned out not to be a sunk cost at all. Those years were what allowed her to sit credibly across from the senior leaders she now coaches, which is to say the practice she wound down kept working for her inside the practice she built.

The people who arrive

It would be easy to file what Whitney does now under career services, and the label would miss most of it. People rarely bring a career to a coach because everything is fine, and the field she serves keeps producing a particular kind of trouble. It is full of accidental leaders, she observes: craft people promoted into managing others because that was the only ladder on offer, now spending their days in meetings, mourning the work their hands used to do. Designers at large, she has noticed, see themselves as problem solvers and business growers and are received as people who make nice things, and they extend endless empathy to their users and almost none to their own kind, or to themselves. “We take a lot of responsibility on our shoulders,” she said of her profession.

So the coaching rarely stays inside the career, because the career is rarely where the trouble actually lives. Her question for clients is not what the next role should be but something quieter and harder: what is their best self, and what would work look like if it were built around it? It is the same instinct that surfaced in her consulting days, the group-therapist tendency she once joked about on her blog, matured into the job itself. It also explains her list of interests better than any career-services framing could. A coach who follows her clients’ troubles all the way down will end up talking about money, about grief, about what remains when the title is gone, which is to say she ends up coaching a life, and the career only as the part of it that happens between nine and five.

In defence of detours

The part of our conversation I have thought about most came when I asked what is next for her. Instead of an answer about deepening the coaching practice, she gave me a list: she is interested in financial advising, in training as an end-of-life doula, and, she added with a smile, in private investigation.

The list sounds eccentric until you trace where each item comes from. The interest in finance grew out of twenty years of running her own business, and out of the money questions her clients keep carrying into sessions, since you cannot coach someone about their career for very long without talking about what the career is for. The doula interest grew out of grief. She lost a few people close to her in recent years, accompanying those endings at close range, and emerged knowing something she could offer other people in the hardest passage of their lives. Even the private investigator idea, the one that made us both laugh, is her day job wearing a trench coat: she is paid to read systems, incentives, and decision makers, and to notice what everyone in the room is leaving unsaid.

None of these are exits, in other words. They are continuations, experiences she already owns waiting for a context that wants them. Underneath them sits a view of careers that is quietly radical: a working life is not a ladder within one profession but a body of accumulated experience that can be recombined, more than once, into new work. “The decisions that we make now become the legacy that we leave,” she said at one point, and the word legacy is doing real work in that sentence. She thinks about careers on the scale of a whole life, endings included, which may be why becoming a doula does not strike her as a change of subject.

Held up to that light, your own history gets interesting quickly. The banking designer who has spent five years inside compliance reviews is, whether she thinks of it this way or not, becoming an expert in regulated systems. The design lead who has survived three reorganizations has learned things about organizations that consultants charge for. We rarely see this in ourselves, because we are looking at our job titles, and a job title is a summary written by someone else, for a purpose that was never ours.

Where you plant yourself

None of this means growth is purely a matter of will, and the sentence that gave this piece its title was about the limits of it. “You can’t grow roses in a cornfield” Whitney said. Your ability to grow depends to an uncomfortable degree on the environment you are planted in. A cornfield is not hostile; it is optimized for corn. An organization that understands design as decoration will not, through any effort of yours, come to understand it as systems thinking, and the career path available to you inside any company is a function of how mature its design practice is, rather than of what your ambition deserves. Careers, in her telling, transfer no better than components do. “You cannot design one widget and expect it to work in every app in the app store,” she said.

The biggest decision they need to make is where they plant themselves.

Her practical advice follows from the metaphor. “The biggest decision they need to make is where they plant themselves,” she said of the designers she coaches, and she talks about that decision the way people talk about buying property: “I wouldn’t buy a house without doing my research on the neighborhood.” Designers, meanwhile, routinely join companies knowing less about the design culture than they would insist on knowing about a place they were going to live. Who does design report to? What happened to the last three senior designers? Does the career ladder exist anywhere outside the recruiting deck, and has anyone actually climbed it? These are questions you can ask in an interview, and asking them tells the company something about you that works in your favor.

Speaking as someone who runs a design team inside a large bank, I can confirm the information is not hidden. People will tell you how design really lives in their organization, sometimes proudly, sometimes bitterly, usually within ten minutes. We run more discovery for a two-week feature than most of us run for a five-year employment decision, and there is no good reason for that asymmetry.

Running discovery on yourself

What I take from Whitney’s story, and what I would like to hand to the designer from my mentoring call and to everyone quietly carrying some version of her whisper, is not reassurance. The market is hard at the entry level, unstable in the middle, and strange at the top, and reassurance would be a kind of lie. What her story offers instead is a method, and it is one designers already practice daily on other people’s problems.

It begins with discovery, pointed inward. The research question is not which job titles you could plausibly get. It is which moments of the past five years felt like yours, and what people keep bringing to you that appears nowhere in your job description. Whitney’s whisper named the facilitator inside the problem solver. Yours is likely to be similarly specific, if you give it the kind of patient attention you would give a user interview.

It continues with an inventory. Somewhere in your history is experience that feels off-topic: the failed side business, the caregiving years, the community you moderate, the domain you absorbed by accident. On the ladder model of a career this is clutter. On Whitney’s model it is material, and some of it is closer to becoming work than you think.

Then comes the audit of the soil, which is the uncomfortable step, because it can return the finding that nothing is wrong with you while something is wrong with the field you are planted in. The move that follows is not necessarily out of design. Sometimes it is only out of the cornfield.

And then you prototype, cheaply and early, the way she did both times. The consulting business ran for three years on the side before she trusted it with her livelihood, and the coaching practice ramped up while consulting still paid the bills. The jumps were real, but each was the last step of a long prototype rather than the first step of a plan. Mentoring one person, taking one course, writing one essay: these are the paper prototypes of a next career, and they cost about as much as paper.

What holds it together is the kickoff feeling, that trained confidence in your own resourcefulness. It is not Whitney’s private gift. It belongs to the profession, built into all of us by every project that started in fog and ended in shipping. UX has always attracted people who want their work to mean something, and that appetite survives any particular job, which is exactly why it aches when the job stops feeding it.

A question for a slow afternoon

Near the end of our call Whitney said she wants to keep developing her skills “over the arc of my career,” and it was clear she meant the arc of a working life, forty-some years across however many professions those years turn out to contain. She likes variety, she told me: “I like having every day feel different.” “Life happens,” she reminded me. “All your life plans go out the window. Covid happens.” What survives is the why underneath, the boundaries you will not trade away, and a flexibility about nearly everything else, so that when an opening appears you are able to recognize it and move.

We need to be connected with our WHY.

I think about my mentee often. The tears were not a breakdown, as far as I can tell. They were information arriving, a whisper that had been ignored long enough to find another channel, and the kindest thing that moment did was make the question impossible to postpone any further.

So, in the spirit of the season, and with whatever slow afternoon you can find: what do you actually love doing? Not what you are good at, which is a different list, and not what pays, which is a third. If you trusted yourself the way you trust yourself at every kickoff, what would you scope first? Somewhere inside the job you have is the work you want, and finding it is not a leap of faith. It is a design problem, and you have been training for it your whole career.

Whitney Hess coaches creative leaders at whitneyhess.com. Her 2012 essay “Designing the Company, Not the Product” is where this story quietly begins.

This conversation is part of a series of interviews with designers who left the craft or reshaped it into something new, for a book in progress.

If the soil audit above left you wondering where you actually stand, I built a tool for that step: a free, scenario based self assessment, about ten minutes, and the output is a profile, not a grade. Treat it as a private room. You can take it at designlevel.io/assessment

And if you think I am wrong about any of this, tell me. The strongest corrections to my thinking have come from readers.

You can’t grow roses in a cornfield was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
